name: Catherine the Great
info: Catherine II, born the German princess Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst in 1729, overthrew her husband Peter III in 1762 and ruled Russia as empress until 1796, expanding the empire and presiding over the Russian Enlightenment.

facts.born: 2 May 1729 in Stettin (now Szczecin), Pomerania, Kingdom of Prussia, as Princess Sophie Auguste Friederike von Anhalt-Zerbst; daughter of Christian August, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, and Joanna Elisabeth of Holstein-Gottorp
facts.died: 17 November 1796, the evening after a stroke that left her in a coma; an autopsy confirmed the stroke as the cause
facts.role: Grand duchess as wife of the heir Peter (from 1745); empress consort (1762); Empress of Russia from 9 July 1762 until her death in 1796
facts.known: the coup of 1762 against Peter III; wars with the Ottoman Empire and the annexation of Crimea in 1783; the partitions of Poland; the provincial reform of 1775 and the charters of 1785; the secularisation of Church lands; the Smolny Institute and a state school system; the Hermitage; her correspondence with Voltaire

t: A German princess with no claim to the Russian throne, Catherine took it in 1762 by a coup against her husband Peter III, who died eight days later in unexplained circumstances.

In a reign of over 34 years she extended the empire by some 520,000 square kilometres at the expense mainly of the Ottoman Empire and the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth, and reorganised provincial government, education and Church property.
She brought the abolition of serfdom into public debate, but the exploitation of serf labour intensified under her and was one of the chief reasons behind Pugachev's Rebellion.
dyk: To promote smallpox inoculation, then a controversial method, Catherine had herself inoculated in 1768 by the English doctor Thomas Dimsdale; by 1800 approximately 2 million inoculations had been administered in the Russian Empire.
ev: Sophie of Anhalt-Zerbst, the future Catherine, is born in Stettin, where her father is governor
Having been received into the Orthodox Church as Catherine the year before, she marries the heir to the Russian throne, the future Peter III
With the support of guards regiments she overthrows Peter III six months after his accession and begins her reign as Catherine II
She secularises the lands of the Russian Orthodox Church and has her former lover Stanislaus Augustus Poniatowski placed on the Polish throne
The Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca ends a victorious war with the Ottoman Empire; Pugachev's Rebellion spreads among serfs and peasants
Catherine annexes Crimea, and Georgia becomes a Russian protectorate by the Treaty of Georgievsk
Russia, Prussia and Austria divide the remaining territory of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in the third partition
Catherine suffers a stroke and dies the following evening; her son succeeds as Paul I

sections.early:
Catherine was born on 2 May 1729 as Princess Sophie Auguste Friederike von Anhalt-Zerbst in Stettin, in Prussian Pomerania. Her father, Christian August, Prince of Anhalt-Zerbst, of the ruling German family of Anhalt, was a Prussian general and governor of the city; her mother was Joanna Elisabeth of Holstein-Gottorp. The family had little money, and her rise was supported by her mother's wealthy relatives. Among the more than 300 sovereign entities of the Holy Roman Empire, small princely families advanced themselves by marriage, and Sophie was groomed throughout her childhood to become the wife of a powerful ruler. She was taught chiefly by a French governess and tutors, in etiquette, French and Lutheran theology. In 1739, aged ten, she met her second cousin, the future Peter III of Russia, whom she later wrote that she found detestable.

Her selection as bride of the heir was bound up with a diplomatic intrigue meant to strengthen the friendship of Prussia and Russia. She arrived in Russia in 1744, aged 15, and set out to win the Empress Elizabeth and the Russian people, studying Russian late into the night. During a grave illness she asked for an Orthodox priest rather than a Lutheran pastor, which raised her standing at court. Against her father's objections she was received into the Russian Orthodox Church on 28 June 1744, taking the name Catherine Alekseyevna. She married Peter on 21 August 1745 in Saint Petersburg. Elizabeth expelled her mother from the country amid allegations of spying for Frederick the Great of Prussia.
sections.rise:
The marriage was unsuccessful and, by the usual account, remained unconsummated for years. The couple lived at Oranienbaum, where from 1746 Elizabeth placed Catherine under a supervision that one historian, Dixon, compares to virtual house arrest. Catherine read widely in French, among others Voltaire and Tacitus. She took lovers, among them Sergei Saltykov, Stanislaus Augustus Poniatowski and from 1759 the officer Grigory Orlov. Her son Paul was born in 1754 and taken into Elizabeth's care; the first version of her memoirs strongly implies that his father was Saltykov, while the final version explains why he was Peter's son. She gained political allies, among them the chancellor Alexey Bestuzhev-Ryumin, whose arrest in 1758 exposed her to scrutiny.

Elizabeth died on 5 January 1762 and Peter became emperor. His admiration for Frederick II, against whom Russia had been fighting, his ending of operations against Prussia and his planned war on Denmark alienated the groups Catherine had cultivated. On the night of 8 July 1762 she learned that a co-conspirator had been arrested and that the coup must take place at once. The next day she went to the Izmailovsky Regiment and asked the soldiers to protect her, and then to the Semenovsky Barracks, where the clergy were waiting. She had Peter arrested and made him sign an abdication. On 17 July he died at Ropsha, possibly at the hands of Alexei Orlov; how he died is unknown, and the official cause was haemorrhoidal colic and a stroke. She was crowned in Moscow on 22 September 1762.
sections.deeds:
Catherine extended the empire by some 520,000 square kilometres. The Russo-Turkish War of 1768–1774, with victories at Chesma and Kagul in 1770, ended in the Treaty of Küçük Kaynarca, which gave Russia territories on the Black Sea coast and the position of protector of Orthodox Christians in the Ottoman Empire. She annexed Crimea in 1783, and a second war ended with the Treaty of Jassy in 1792. Cities such as Kherson, Nikolayev, Yekaterinoslav and Odessa were founded in the south. In Poland she placed Poniatowski on the throne in 1764 and shared in the partitions of 1772, 1793 and 1795. Georgia became a protectorate in 1783, and she mediated in the War of the Bavarian Succession.

In 1766 she summoned a commission of 652 members of all classes and wrote for it an Instruction drawn, as she admitted, from Montesquieu and Beccaria; it dissolved after more than 200 sittings without getting beyond theory. The Statute on provincial administration of 1775 divided the country into provinces and districts, 50 and nearly 500 by the end of the reign. In 1785 she issued the Charter to the Nobility and the Charter of the Towns. A decree of 1764 transferred the Church's estates, with more than 911,000 registered male peasants, to the treasury.

She founded the Smolny Institute in 1764, approved a Statute of National Schools in 1786, under which the recorded schools rose to 316 with 17,341 pupils by 1796, permitted private printing houses in 1783, issued the first government paper money and began the Hermitage as her own collection. She corresponded with Voltaire for 15 years.
sections.opponents:
Catherine's title was disputed from the start; historians debate whether her status was that of a regent or a usurper, tolerable only in her son's minority. Ivan VI, confined since infancy, was killed during an attempt to free him, on standing instructions she had given, as Elizabeth had before her. The greatest revolt was that of Pugachev, who claimed to be Peter III and drew Cossacks, nomads, peoples of the Volga and peasants in 1774. Its causes lay in serfdom: the demands of state and landowners intensified the exploitation of serf labour, and nobles gained the power to send serfs to hard labour in Siberia. Catherine forbade serfs to petition her directly, and gave away serfs in great numbers, 100,000 on one day in 1795. After the uprising she was pushed away from the idea of liberation.

When Alexander Radishchev published his Journey from St. Petersburg to Moscow in 1790, warning of uprisings over the condition of the serfs, she had the book burned and the author exiled to Siberia. She deported over 20,000 Old Believers to Siberia in 1764, closed 569 of 954 monasteries, confined the Jews acquired with Polish lands to the Pale of Settlement and taxed them at double the rate of their Orthodox neighbours. In Poland her protectorate provoked the Confederation of Bar and, in 1794, the Kościuszko Uprising, both defeated.

The British ambassador James Harris credited her with a “masculine force of mind” but charged her with vanity and love of flattery. Her grandson Nicholas I judged her foreign policy dishonest, and it is criticised as lacking a long-term strategy.
sections.last:
In her last years Catherine's favourite was Platon Zubov, 40 years her junior. Grigory Potemkin, her lover and adviser, who had governed the colonisation of New Russia, had died in 1791. In 1796 she made war on Persia, whose new king Agha Mohammad Khan had invaded Georgia in 1795; on Zubov's advice she gave the command not to the seasoned general Ivan Gudovich but to Zubov's youthful brother Valerian, whose troops stormed Derbent in May and by mid-June had overrun most of modern Azerbaijan.

Her reign ended in two failures. In September 1796 the Swedish king Gustav IV Adolf visited her, and she intended her granddaughter Alexandra to become queen of Sweden. He would not accept that Alexandra would remain Orthodox, stayed away from the ball of 11 September at which the engagement was to be announced, and left for Stockholm. The frustration affected Catherine's health. She recovered enough to plan a ceremony naming her favourite grandson Alexander as heir in place of her son Paul, but died before it could be announced.

On 16 November 1796 she rose early, took her coffee and sat down to her papers. Some time after nine she was found on the floor, her face purplish and her breathing laboured. The court physician diagnosed a stroke; she fell into a coma, received the last rites and died the following evening at about 9:45. An autopsy confirmed the cause. She was laid out with a gold crown on her head, in a silver brocade dress. Paul succeeded her and ordered the army in the Caucasus to retreat to Russia.
sections.legacy:
Under Catherine the Russian Empire was recognised as a great power of Europe, and she is often counted among the enlightened despots. Poland ceased to exist as an independent nation until after the First World War. The decline of Ottoman power opened the European contest over the Eastern Question, which lasted until that empire's dissolution. Paul's reversal of the Persian campaign embittered the Zubovs and other officers, many of whom were among the conspirators who arranged his murder five years later.

Her institutions outlasted her. The provincial boards of public welfare, the foundling homes and the school statute of 1786 gave public education a legal and administrative foundation for the nineteenth century, though the schools excluded serfs and most rural inhabitants had little access to them. The assignation roubles she introduced circulated until 1849. The Hermitage, begun as her personal collection, now occupies the whole Winter Palace, and the Imperial Public Library she founded in 1795 opened in 1814. Writers of her reign such as Derzhavin and Fonvizin prepared the ground for Pushkin.

Voltaire, Diderot and d'Alembert cemented her reputation in their writings; Voltaire called her the “Star of the North”. Her sexual independence gave rise to many legends. Historians regard her promotion of inoculation as one of her most significant contributions, and note that she was the first Russian ruler to bring the abolition of serfdom into public debate while her economy and army continued to depend on it.

summary: Catherine II (1729–1796), a German princess married to the heir to the Russian throne, overthrew her husband Peter III in 1762 and ruled for over 34 years. She expanded Russia to the Black Sea and into Poland and reformed provincial government, schools and Church property, while serfdom grew harsher and provoked Pugachev's Rebellion.
references: John Alexander, Catherine the Great: Life and Legend (Oxford University Press, 1989)
Isabel De Madariaga, Russia in the Age of Catherine the Great (Yale University Press, 1981)
Robert K. Massie, Catherine the Great: Portrait of a Woman (Random House, 2011)
Virginia Rounding, Catherine the Great: Love, Sex and Power (Hutchinson, 2006)
notes: Dates are New Style as the article gives them first (coup 8-9 July 1762, OS 27-28 June; the Orlov section calls it 'the 28 June 1762 coup'). Church reception 28 June 1744, decree on Church lands 26 February 1764 and school statute 5 August 1786 are given in the article as Old Style or unmarked.

Death: the lede gives 17 November 1796; the body says the stroke was on 16 November [O.S. 5 November] and she died 'the following evening'. Consistent. The article does not name the place of death (no palace or city is stated), so facts.died has none.

Legislative Commission: the article says 'Four years later, in 1766' she called the Grand Commission, and elsewhere speaks of 'the Legislative Commission of 1767'; 1766 used in 'deeds', not made an event.

Pugachev: the article says 'Pugachev's Rebellion of 1774' and also that it was 'starting to take root' by the winter of 1773; the Potemkin section dates a letter about the Volga uprising to 1772 (doubtful). Event dated 1774.
Illness on arrival: the article gives both 'pneumonia' and 'a pleuritis'; 'a grave illness' used.

Paul's paternity: the article gives both versions of the memoirs; both stated. 'By the usual account' for the unconsummated marriage reflects the article's attribution to Peter's 'mental immaturity' and Catherine's later claim.
Charter of the Towns: dated 1785 in most passages, '1782' in the Judaism section; 1785 used.
Religion in schools: one section says the 1786 statute kept Christian instruction, another that 'by 1786, Catherine excluded all religion and clerical studies programs from lay education'; left out.
Odessa is listed among cities founded (one passage) and as replacing Khadjibey by decree in 1794; Sevastopol appears only in the lede's list.

The paragraph 'The evaluation of foreign policy' is unsourced in tone (famines, the dynasty's fall blamed on her policy); only Nicholas I's judgement and 'lacking a long-term strategy' are used, attributed generally.

The horse rumour is named in the article; here only 'rumours about the manner of her death'. The article gives no burial place, and the Issue section is a heading only. Dixon's first name is not given in the article.
Serf figures used: 100,000 given away on 18 August 1795; others (66,000 in 1762-1772; 202,000 in 1773-1793; 500,000 owned) left out for space.
References: books about the person from the article's own bibliography sections (scripts/kinds/article-refs.js, or its Further reading list), chosen by the editor.
